units.title: Foundations of Scholarly Reading & Writing
units.question: How do careful readers turn observations into defensible ideas?
units.summary: Establish annotation, inference, paragraph architecture, grammar control, academic integrity, and productive revision habits.
units.texts: Original course texts, short public-domain essays, selected speeches, and teacher-approved informational passages.
units.assessment: Evidence-based analytical paragraph, revised diagnostic essay, and language conventions check.

units.title: Myth, Epic & Archetype
units.question: How do cultures use stories to explain duty, identity, power, and the unknown?
units.summary: Compare origin stories, heroic patterns, archetypes, cultural values, and transformations of source material across civilizations.
units.texts: The Epic of Gilgamesh, The Odyssey, Popol Vuh, and teacher-selected passages from African, Asian, Indigenous, and Near Eastern traditions.
units.assessment: Comparative literary analysis with a visual archetype map.

units.title: Short Fiction & Narrative Craft
units.question: How do writers shape a reader’s experience through character, structure, perspective, and detail?
units.summary: Study character, conflict, setting, point of view, irony, pacing, dialogue, and the deliberate revision of original fiction.
units.texts: Public-domain short fiction by writers such as Edgar Allan Poe, Kate Chopin, Anton Chekhov, Rabindranath Tagore, and Ryūnosuke Akutagawa.
units.assessment: Polished short story with craft commentary and peer-review record.

units.title: Poetry, Voice & Form
units.question: How can compressed language carry sound, image, argument, memory, and emotion?
units.summary: Analyze imagery, diction, figurative language, rhythm, meter, form, translation, and performance while composing an original portfolio.
units.texts: Public-domain poetry by Shakespeare, Dickinson, Whitman, Dunbar, Bashō, Li Bai in approved translation, and other global poets.
units.assessment: Four-poem portfolio, comparative analysis, and formal oral reading.

units.title: Drama, Choice & Consequence
units.question: How does drama place competing duties, values, and consequences into public view?
units.summary: Read drama as literature and performance, examining dramatic structure, stagecraft, character motivation, conflict, and interpretation.
units.texts: Sophocles’ Antigone or Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, with shorter scenes from world drama.
units.assessment: Literary analysis, Socratic seminar, and staged interpretation.

units.title: Rhetoric & Public Voice
units.question: How do speakers use language, evidence, structure, and delivery to move an audience?
units.summary: Introduce rhetorical situation, ethos, pathos, logos, claims, reasoning, fallacies, style, speech writing, and purposeful delivery.
units.texts: Public-domain speeches and essays by Frederick Douglass, Sojourner Truth, Abraham Lincoln, Theodore Roosevelt, and other civic voices.
units.assessment: Four-to-six-minute evidence-based speech with rhetorical analysis.

units.title: Research, Evidence & Media Literacy
units.question: How can researchers find, test, connect, and ethically present reliable information?
units.summary: Build research questions, advanced search plans, lateral-reading habits, source evaluations, annotations, citations, and synthesized reports.
units.texts: Current and historical informational sources selected through The Verifier, PLERA Search, ARSHIF, and public archives.
units.assessment: Annotated bibliography, source audit, and 900–1,200-word research report.

units.title: Informational & Technical Communication
units.question: How do writers make complex processes and ideas accurate, usable, and clear?
units.summary: Study explanatory structures, definitions, classification, cause and effect, technical procedures, data displays, captions, and visual rhetoric.
units.texts: Science, environment, health, technology, and public-information texts drawn from the Verve N Veda learning network.
units.assessment: Explanatory article, tested procedure, and accessible infographic.

units.title: The Novel & Sustained Inquiry
units.question: What becomes visible when a reader follows characters, patterns, and ideas across an entire book?
units.summary: Sustain independent reading, track motifs and character arcs, build contextual knowledge, compare interpretations, and write a developed analysis.
units.texts: One teacher-approved full novel, with public-domain choices including Frankenstein, Jane Eyre, The Time Machine, or The Call of the Wild.
units.assessment: 1,200–1,500-word literary analysis and independent reading conference.

units.title: Argument, Debate & Civic Reasoning
units.question: What makes an argument fair, rigorous, responsive, and persuasive?
units.summary: Frame issues, distinguish claims from assumptions, test evidence, address counterclaims, rebut respectfully, debate, and revise position papers.
units.texts: Paired arguments, policy excerpts, civic documents, editorials, and evidence sets selected for balance and source transparency.

units.title: Creative Media & Publication
units.question: How do words, images, sound, layout, and sequence work together for a real audience?
units.summary: Plan a publication, study visual rhetoric and editorial design, revise collaboratively, credit sources, and produce a literary magazine or exhibit.
units.texts: Student-selected mentor texts, visual essays, poems, short nonfiction, art criticism, and multimedia compositions.
units.assessment: Curated literary magazine, digital exhibit, or themed publication with editorial statement.

units.title: Capstone Portfolio & Oral Defense
units.question: How can a student demonstrate growth, judgment, independence, and a distinctive command of language?
units.summary: Curate a standards-based portfolio, revise major works, complete a synthesis capstone, sit for a cumulative examination, and defend learning orally.
units.texts: The student’s complete body of Grade 9 work, selected mentor texts, research sources, and reflective evidence.
units.assessment: Portfolio, synthesis capstone, cumulative final examination, and oral defense.

weekPlans.title: Diagnostic Reading & Writer Identity
weekPlans.question: What do my present reading and writing habits reveal?
weekPlans.reading: Original diagnostic passage and a personal literacy inventory.
weekPlans.writing: Write a controlled baseline essay and identify one measurable growth goal.
weekPlans.product: Revised diagnostic essay with self-assessment.

weekPlans.title: Close Reading, Claims & Evidence
weekPlans.question: How does a reader move from detail to inference?
weekPlans.reading: Short literary and informational passages with layered details.
weekPlans.writing: Build claim-evidence-reasoning paragraphs with precise quotations.
weekPlans.product: Two polished evidence paragraphs and an annotation sample.

weekPlans.title: Revision, Style & Academic Integrity
weekPlans.question: What changes make writing clearer, stronger, and more trustworthy?
weekPlans.reading: Before-and-after drafts, paraphrases, summaries, and source notes.
weekPlans.writing: Revise for focus, coherence, sentence variety, attribution, and citation.
weekPlans.product: Unit 1 mastery task and conventions check.

weekPlans.title: Why Humans Make Myths
weekPlans.question: What work does myth perform in a culture?
weekPlans.reading: Creation, flood, trickster, and transformation narratives from several traditions.
weekPlans.writing: Explain how a myth encodes values through pattern and symbol.
weekPlans.product: Cultural-function analysis paragraph and archetype chart.

weekPlans.title: Epic Heroes & Cultural Values
weekPlans.question: How does an epic hero embody and challenge communal ideals?
weekPlans.reading: Episodes from Gilgamesh and The Odyssey with contextual notes.
weekPlans.writing: Compare heroic traits, tests, consequences, and cultural expectations.
weekPlans.grammar: verb tense consistency and active voice
weekPlans.product: Comparative evidence matrix and timed analysis.

weekPlans.title: Comparative Myth Synthesis
weekPlans.question: How can two traditions illuminate one another without being flattened into sameness?
weekPlans.reading: Paired myths with attention to historical and cultural context.
weekPlans.writing: Write a comparative thesis and organize evidence by meaningful criteria.
weekPlans.product: Comparative literary essay and visual archetype map.

weekPlans.title: Character, Conflict & Setting
weekPlans.question: How do setting and conflict pressure a character into revealing values?
weekPlans.reading: Public-domain short fiction with contrasting settings and conflicts.
weekPlans.writing: Analyze direct and indirect characterization; draft a scene with a decisive turn.
weekPlans.product: Character analysis and original scene.

weekPlans.title: Point of View, Structure & Irony
weekPlans.question: How does the arrangement of information shape a reader’s judgment?
weekPlans.reading: Stories using first person, limited third person, frames, and irony.
weekPlans.writing: Explain the effects of perspective and restructure a scene from another viewpoint.
weekPlans.grammar: pronoun case and shifts in person
weekPlans.product: Perspective analysis and rewritten scene.

weekPlans.title: Narrative Workshop
weekPlans.question: What makes a short story purposeful rather than merely eventful?
weekPlans.reading: Mentor openings, dialogue passages, endings, and revision models.
weekPlans.writing: Draft, conference, revise, proofread, and annotate an original short story.
weekPlans.product: Polished short story with craft commentary.

weekPlans.title: Image, Diction & Figurative Language
weekPlans.question: How does a poet make an idea sensuous and memorable?
weekPlans.reading: Short lyric poems across periods and cultures.
weekPlans.writing: Analyze word choice and imagery; write image-rich free verse.
weekPlans.product: Close-reading annotation and two original poems.

weekPlans.title: Sound, Rhythm & Form
weekPlans.question: How do sound and structure create expectation and emphasis?
weekPlans.reading: Sonnets, ballads, odes, haiku, blank verse, and free verse.
weekPlans.writing: Scan selected lines and experiment with a received form.
weekPlans.grammar: syntax for emphasis and purposeful inversion
weekPlans.product: Formal poem and craft explanation.

weekPlans.title: Comparison, Translation & Performance
weekPlans.question: What is gained, changed, or contested when poetry is translated and performed?
weekPlans.reading: Paired translations and recorded or live readings.
weekPlans.writing: Compare translations and prepare an expressive oral interpretation.
weekPlans.grammar: punctuation as a guide to voice and pace
weekPlans.product: Poetry portfolio, comparison, and oral reading.

weekPlans.title: Reading Drama as Literature and Performance
weekPlans.question: How does a play communicate through words, bodies, space, and silence?
weekPlans.reading: Opening scenes, stage directions, and performance choices.
weekPlans.writing: Annotate a scene for conflict, blocking, subtext, and audience knowledge.
weekPlans.product: Director’s notebook and scene analysis.

weekPlans.title: Duty, Power & Consequence
weekPlans.question: When obligations conflict, how should a person decide?
weekPlans.reading: A sustained reading of Antigone or Julius Caesar.
weekPlans.writing: Trace a character’s reasoning and evaluate competing claims using the text.
weekPlans.product: Character-argument map and literary analysis draft.

weekPlans.title: Seminar & Dramatic Interpretation
weekPlans.question: How can interpretation remain creative while accountable to evidence?
weekPlans.reading: Critical questions, alternate stagings, and key scenes.
weekPlans.writing: Revise analysis, participate in seminar, and stage a scene with rationale.
weekPlans.product: Final drama essay, seminar, and performance.

weekPlans.title: The Rhetorical Situation
weekPlans.question: How do audience, purpose, context, and occasion shape a message?
weekPlans.reading: Public-domain speeches, letters, and essays.
weekPlans.writing: Identify rhetorical situations and imitate one effective strategy for a new audience.
weekPlans.product: Rhetorical précis and imitation paragraph.

weekPlans.title: Reasoning, Evidence & Fallacies
weekPlans.question: How can a reader test whether persuasion is responsible and sound?
weekPlans.reading: Arguments with strong and weak reasoning.
weekPlans.writing: Map claims, evidence, assumptions, counterclaims, and common fallacies.
weekPlans.product: Argument map and fallacy correction task.

weekPlans.title: Speech Writing & Delivery
weekPlans.question: How does a writer compose language meant to be heard once?
weekPlans.reading: Model openings, repetitions, transitions, evidence, and conclusions.
weekPlans.writing: Draft, rehearse, revise, and deliver an evidence-based speech.
weekPlans.product: Four-to-six-minute speech and rhetorical reflection.

weekPlans.title: Research Questions & Search Strategy
weekPlans.question: What makes a research question focused, significant, and answerable?
weekPlans.reading: Background sources, reference entries, and search-result sets.
weekPlans.writing: Move from topic to inquiry; build keyword, synonym, and source-type plans.
weekPlans.product: Research proposal and search log.

weekPlans.title: Credibility, Bias & Lateral Reading
weekPlans.question: How can a researcher investigate a source instead of merely reading it?
weekPlans.reading: Web pages, articles, data displays, and source histories.
weekPlans.writing: Verify authorship, funding, evidence, date, context, and corroboration.
weekPlans.product: Three-source credibility audit.

weekPlans.title: Synthesis, Citation & Research Reporting
weekPlans.question: How do researchers create a new understanding from multiple sources?
weekPlans.reading: Source clusters representing complementary and conflicting evidence.
weekPlans.writing: Integrate summary, paraphrase, quotation, citation, and analysis.
weekPlans.grammar: embedding quotations and avoiding dangling quotations
weekPlans.product: Annotated bibliography and mini research report.

weekPlans.title: Structures of Explanation
weekPlans.question: Which structure best helps a reader understand a complex idea?
weekPlans.reading: Definition, classification, sequence, comparison, and cause-effect texts.
weekPlans.writing: Plan and draft an explanation using headings, examples, and purposeful structure.
weekPlans.product: Explanatory article outline and first draft.

weekPlans.title: Technical Reading & Procedural Writing
weekPlans.question: How can a writer make a process accurate, safe, and reproducible?
weekPlans.reading: Instructions, diagrams, specifications, safety notes, and troubleshooting guides.
weekPlans.writing: Write a procedure, test it with a user, record failures, and revise.
weekPlans.grammar: imperative mood, conditionals, and precise modifiers
weekPlans.product: Tested procedure with revision log.

weekPlans.title: Data, Visuals & Accessible Information
weekPlans.question: How should words and visuals divide the work of explanation?
weekPlans.reading: Charts, captions, infographics, diagrams, and accessible design examples.
weekPlans.writing: Integrate verified data, captions, alt text, visual hierarchy, and source credit.
weekPlans.grammar: numbers, units, captions, and consistent terminology
weekPlans.product: Final explanatory article and infographic.

weekPlans.title: Launching a Sustained Novel Study
weekPlans.question: How can readers maintain attention, questions, and evidence across a long text?
weekPlans.reading: Opening chapters, context sources, and a full-book reading calendar.
weekPlans.writing: Establish a reading notebook and develop questions that can grow over time.
weekPlans.product: Reading plan, context note, and first conference.

weekPlans.title: Character Arcs, Motifs & Themes
weekPlans.question: How do repeated details gather meaning across a novel?
weekPlans.reading: Middle sections of the selected novel and related context.
weekPlans.writing: Track changes, patterns, contradictions, and competing interpretations.
weekPlans.product: Pattern tracker and analytical notebook entry.

weekPlans.title: Critical Perspectives & Literary Analysis
weekPlans.question: How can a critical lens clarify a text without replacing the text?
weekPlans.reading: Final chapters, reviews, and short contextual perspectives.
weekPlans.writing: Develop, draft, conference, and revise a sustained literary argument.
weekPlans.grammar: cohesion, transitions, and precise analytical verbs
weekPlans.product: Literary analysis and reading conference.

weekPlans.title: Issue Framing & Counterclaims
weekPlans.question: How does the way an issue is framed influence possible conclusions?
weekPlans.reading: Balanced issue sets with definitions, histories, and stakeholder views.
weekPlans.writing: Define terms, narrow a claim, identify stakeholders, and represent opposition fairly.
weekPlans.product: Issue brief and provisional thesis.

weekPlans.title: Evidence, Rebuttal & Ethical Persuasion
weekPlans.question: What evidence is sufficient, relevant, representative, and ethically used?
weekPlans.reading: Data, testimony, cases, expert analysis, and competing arguments.
weekPlans.writing: Select evidence, explain warrants, concede limits, and rebut responsibly.
weekPlans.product: Evidence dossier and argument draft.

weekPlans.title: Debate & Position Paper
weekPlans.question: How should an argument change after serious engagement with opposition?
weekPlans.reading: Student evidence dossiers and debate briefs.
weekPlans.writing: Debate, evaluate feedback, revise claims, and publish a position paper.
weekPlans.grammar: editing for concision, emphasis, and consistency
weekPlans.product: Structured debate and final position paper.

weekPlans.title: Audience, Genre & Multimodal Composition
weekPlans.question: How does a real audience change what and how a writer creates?
weekPlans.reading: Literary magazines, digital exhibits, visual essays, and audio features.
weekPlans.writing: Define audience, purpose, genre, editorial standards, and production roles.
weekPlans.product: Publication proposal and editorial calendar.

weekPlans.title: Editing, Layout & Visual Rhetoric
weekPlans.question: How do design choices guide attention and shape interpretation?
weekPlans.reading: Layouts, typography, image-text relationships, captions, and credits.
weekPlans.writing: Edit copy, establish hierarchy, commission or create visuals, and test accessibility.
weekPlans.product: Edited spread or digital prototype.

weekPlans.title: Publication Studio
weekPlans.question: What responsibilities accompany publishing work for others to read?
weekPlans.reading: Student submissions, editorial notes, permissions, and final proofs.
weekPlans.writing: Revise collaboratively, verify facts, credit sources, proofread, and publish.
weekPlans.grammar: proofreading systems and final consistency checks
weekPlans.product: Literary magazine or digital exhibit and editorial statement.

weekPlans.title: Portfolio Curation & Reflection
weekPlans.question: What evidence best demonstrates genuine growth rather than simple completion?
weekPlans.reading: The student’s Grade 9 reading, writing, speaking, research, and language record.
weekPlans.writing: Select artifacts, explain growth, identify remaining weaknesses, and revise strategically.
weekPlans.product: Draft standards-based portfolio.

weekPlans.title: Capstone Synthesis Project
weekPlans.question: How can one project integrate literary, informational, research, and creative modes?
weekPlans.reading: Student-selected texts and sources connected by a significant inquiry.
weekPlans.writing: Create a synthesis project with an analytical, research, and creative component.
weekPlans.product: Capstone project and process record.

weekPlans.title: Cumulative Examination & Oral Defense
weekPlans.question: How can a student explain and defend what has been learned?
weekPlans.reading: Unfamiliar literary and informational passages plus the completed portfolio.
weekPlans.writing: Complete the final examination, revise the portfolio, and present an oral defense.
weekPlans.product: Final exam, completed portfolio, and oral defense.
